subject: moving-continents
title: Continental Drift: Right Idea, Missing Mechanism
summary: How evidence from the sea floor turned a rejected idea into plate tectonics.

keys.prompt: Why was continental drift rejected at first, even with good evidence?
keys.answer: It lacked a believable mechanism: Wegener said continents plowed through the sea floor, which solid rock couldn't do.

keys.prompt: What do the magnetic stripes on the sea floor show?
keys.answer: New rock forms at the ridge, records Earth's magnetic field as it cools, and spreads outward, matching on both sides.

keys.prompt: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreads about 2.5 cm a year. Why does that matter?
keys.answer: Over 100 to 200 million years, that slow spreading opened the whole Atlantic Ocean.

cards.title: Rejected, then right
cards.text: In 1912 Alfred Wegener proposed that continents move. Most geologists dismissed the idea. About fifty years later it became the foundation of modern geology. What changed?

cards.question: Wegener's idea had good evidence but was rejected for decades. What do you think finally changed geologists' minds?

options.text: Sea-floor evidence of new rock forming and spreading

cards.reveal: Evidence from the sea floor: magnetic stripes matching on both sides of mid-ocean ridges, then 1968 drill cores from the Glomar Challenger that proved seafloor spreading.

cards.title: The original case
cards.text: Wegener pointed to the fit of South America and Africa, matching fossils on both coasts, and climate clues like coal from tropical plants in Antarctica. His theory said the supercontinent Pangaea began to break up about 200 million years ago.

cards.title: The fatal weakness
cards.text: Critics asked what force could move continents. Wegener said they plowed through the ocean floor. The geophysicist Harold Jeffreys argued, correctly, that solid rock could not plow through the sea floor without breaking up.
cards.example: A theory can have strong evidence and still be rejected if its mechanism is wrong.

cards.title: The sea floor's tape recording
cards.text: In the 1950s, scientists found a zebra pattern of magnetic stripes on the sea floor. The stripes matched on both sides of mid-ocean ridges. New rock forms at the ridge, records Earth's magnetic field as it cools, and moves outward. Rocks get older the farther they are from the ridge.

why.q: Why are rocks older the farther they are from the ridge?
why.a: New rock forms at the ridge and moves outward, so rock far away formed longer ago.

cards.title: Clinching evidence
cards.text: In 1968 the research ship Glomar Challenger drilled sea-floor cores across the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Dating the samples proved seafloor spreading. Today the Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreads about 2.5 centimeters per year.
cards.example: That sounds slow, but over 100 to 200 million years it opened the whole Atlantic Ocean.

cards.prompt: Geologists rejected drift, then changed their minds when sea-floor data came in. Is that confirmation bias, or the cure for it?
cards.model: Mostly the cure: they changed their view when tests that could have failed, the stripes and the drill cores, came out in drift's favor.

cards.question: Wegener was right about drift but wrong about how it worked. Should he get credit? How should science treat ideas with good evidence but a bad explanation?
nudges: Can you name another idea that was dismissed before it was proved?

questions.q: What was the main scientific objection to Wegener's theory?

options.text: No believable force or mechanism to move continents
options.why: Right. His "plowing" idea did not hold up.

options.text: The continents do not fit at all.
options.why: The fit was one of his best clues.

options.text: Fossils did not match across oceans.
options.why: Matching fossils were part of his evidence.

questions.q: What do the magnetic stripes on the sea floor show?

options.text: New rock forms at ridges and spreads outward, recording magnetic field flips.
options.why: Yes. The symmetric stripes are a record of spreading.
They come from magnetic minerals in volcanic rock.
Rocks near the ridge are the youngest.

questions.q: At about 2.5 cm per year, how far does the Mid-Atlantic Ridge spread in a million years?

options.why: Check the conversion: 100,000 cm make a kilometer.
Too much by a factor of 10.

sources.title: Historical perspective (This Dynamic Earth)
sources.supports: Ortelius in 1596; Wegener's 1912 continental drift; matching coastlines and fossils; coal in Antarctica; the missing force; Wegener's death in 1930; the open question of what drives plates.

sources.title: Developing the theory (This Dynamic Earth)
sources.supports: Echo-sounding and the mid-ocean ridge (more than 50,000 km long); thin seafloor sediment found in 1947; zebra-like magnetic striping; seafloor spreading; the 1968 Glomar Challenger drill cores.

sources.title: Understanding plate motions (This Dynamic Earth)
sources.supports: Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreading of about 2.5 cm per year; rates from under 2.5 to over 15 cm per year; the San Andreas Fault at about 5 cm per year.
